newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada unshaken by Helms-Burton twist.
newsitem.headline: Canada unshaken by Helms-Burton twist.

text.p: The Canadian government said on Thursday that its opposition to U.S. anti-Cuba legislation was as strong as ever, despite an agreement by an Italian company to compensate ITT Corp for its Cuban telephone system.
"I don't think Canada's position has been weakened by this," a spokesman for Canada's Trade Department said in a phone interview.
"We feel that the decision by the (U.S.) State Department has done nothing to change the status quo," spokesman Sanjeev Chowdhury said.

Stet International, an Italian telecommunications company, paid ITT US$25 million so that it could continue its involvement in the Cuban telephone system, which ITT built and operated until it was seized by Communist authorities in 1959.
The deal let Stet avoid being hurt by the U.S. Helms-Burton legislation, which allows U.S. nationals to sue foreign firms using their confiscated property in Cuba.
The law also bars senior executives of companies deemed to be "trafficking" in property seized from U.S. nationals in Cuba from entering the United States.
The only companies accused of violating the legislation so far are Stet, Mexico's Grupo Domo and Canadian mining company Sherritt International Corp.

European Union officials said on Thursday that the U.S. State Department's decision to exonerate Stet from liability under the Helms-Burton law showed how toothless the legislation was. But the State Department and Cuban exile groups said the deal proved the law was effective.
Still, the Canadian government said there was no reason for Canadian companies to change the way they were doing business in Cuba.
"Canada supports them in their business ventures in Cuba," trade spokesman Chowdhury said. "We've made our case clear. (Helms-Burton) is a violation of international law and should be repealed."

He said the Canadian government had given Canadian firms the legal tools to fight any action under the Helms-Burton legislation, and the government was talking regularly with the United States to have the legislation repealed.
